...pure ones. In that <note>state</note>, the aspects are clearly seen.
The meaning of the word which is the agent of cognition
Is by no means external,
Because there is no other <note>object</note> and it is not a real entity.
If one establishes that this very intention to speak
Is the indicator,
It is extremely clear as the third characteristic.

If the intention to speak has not become manifest,
The word does not apply.
A lamp itself does not act as an indicator
For blue and other colors through being a sign <note>rather, it functions as a cause of perception</note>.
Because the capability to produce cognition
Has arisen, it is described in that way.
If the indicator is the actual nature of the sign,
Then consider the property of the subject <term>pakshadharmata</term> <gloss>the presence of the reason in the subject</gloss> and so forth.
Why does one not dispute that
In a case where there is no such logical necessity?
Why is that which is grasped by the eye
Not established as having no alternative explanation?
Because it is devoid of the property of the subject,
Therefore, the single-characteristic <note>definition of a sign</note> is inferior.
That which is spoken of as having one aspect
Indicates indeed a two-fold aspect.
By speaking of the two-fold aspects,
The three-fold aspect is shown from the property of the subject.
If it is argued that this is implied
By the sheer impossibility of any other explanation, that is not so.
Because in other cases as well, such as sound,
This very quality of being graspable by the eye would be desired <note>as a sign</note>.
Reasons such as "because he is her son"
Are not incompatible with the discordant class <term>vipaksha</term> <gloss>the counter-example class</gloss>.
Because the exclusion is doubtful,
That <note>reason</note> does not possess the three aspects.
Even if he is the son of her son,
Due to the distinction of causes
Such as actions and food,
In all cases, the entity becomes something else.
This is neither an effect, nor an essential nature <term>svabhava</term> <gloss>inherent existence</gloss>,
Nor is it the non-perception of the visible.
If it were not distinct from those,
It would be completely unerring.
If it were indeed unerring,
It would be seen in other things as well.
For example, the rising of the moon is the sign
For the opening of the water-lily <term>kumuda</term> and the rising of the tide;
And from seeing the presence of heat,
One thoroughly knows that a shadow
Exists in another part.
By seeing a burning firebrand in the dark,
One infers smoke from afar.
Also, from the rising of the Pleiades <term>Krittika</term>,
One understands that Aldebaran <term>Rohini</term> is near.
In this regard, that property of the reason
Is understood in such a manner.

<summary>This page analyzes the nature of logical signs, the three characteristics of a valid reason, and critiques insufficient definitions of logical evidence while illustrating valid inferences using celestial and elemental examples.</summary>
<keywords>three characteristics of a reason, pakshadharmata, vipaksha, inference, Krittika, Rohini, Indian logic</keywords>

### Fascicle Two

By stating the presence of the reason in the subject <note>the subject of the thesis, original: "phyogs kyi chos", Sanskrit: "pakṣadharmatā"</note> and the positive and negative concomitances <note>concomitance: the necessary connection between the reason and the thesis; original: "rjes su 'gro ldog", Sanskrit: "anvaya-vyatireka"</note>, this text explains both the ascertainment of the positive and negative concomitances as well as the ascertainment of the presence of the reason in the subject. Because the methods of ascertainment are similar, the positive and negative concomitances are explained by distinguishing them from the presence of the reason in the subject itself. 

Here, it is not meant that the positive and negative concomitances are merely explained. In a context where understanding one thing leads to the understanding of another, it is correct to speak in this manner. However, once that which specifically expresses a certain point has been explained, to state it again in this way would not be meaningful. 

If you ask: "Even if one understands the pervasion <note>pervasion: the logical implication where the presence of the reason guarantees the presence of the thesis; original: "khyab pa", Sanskrit: "vyāpti"</note> by that property, is it not for the sake of expressing it?" 

It is not so, because they are understood in the manner that their nature is expressed by passages starting with "pervasion is..." and so forth. If there were some other understanding regarding the presence of the reason in the subject itself, how could it be said that "the presence of the reason in the subject is also explained"? Therefore, even if the word "ascertainment" is not explicitly mentioned, this very meaning—that it is indeed the ascertainment itself that is expressed—is presented here.

If you ask: "What kind of ascertainment is there here?" 

In order to include those three aspects <note>the three conditions of a valid reason; original: "tshul gsum", Sanskrit: "trirūpa"</note> where that exists, the text says "those." The presence of the reason in the subject and the pervasion by that property are the three types of reasons characterized by the effect <note>original: "'bras bu", Sanskrit: "kārya"</note>, the essential nature <note>original: "rang bzhin", Sanskrit: "svabhāva"</note>, and non-cognition <note>original: "mi dmigs pa", Sanskrit: "anupalabdhi"</note>. 

When demonstrating these three stated reasons through examples, how the three—the effect and so forth—are "this and this" is explained in the section starting from "for example" up to the words "is explained." 

Therefore, following the stated order:
1. First, the effect is presented.
2. Second is the essential nature.
3. Finally, non-cognition.

The presentation of both the reason <note>original: "gtan tshigs", Sanskrit: "hetu"</note> and the thesis to be proven <note>original: "bsgrub bya", Sanskrit: "sādhya"</note> is for the purpose of demonstrating the actual relationship of cause and effect. 

The reason of essential nature is, for example: "because it is a Simsapa <note>a species of Ashoka tree; original: "shing sha pa", Sanskrit: "śiṃśapā"</note>." Here too, the presentation of both <note>the reason and the thesis</note> is for the purpose of thoroughly demonstrating the reason as being of the essential nature itself, because those two are established as sharing a single identity.
